One thing people often don't seem to know is how Windows handles file permissions in the "Program Files (x86)" directory. A lot of older games existed in the days where you could pretty much write anywhere you wanted without having to worry about permissions. Most programs kept configuration data and other details inside their program directory. Times have changed. Modern games and programs are expected to keep program configuration and save data in your user profile directories away from the game itself.

These days the "Program Files (x86)" directory requires elevated permissions to write to it. If you have UAC enabled (and you should, this is an important security feature) Windows will ask for elevated permission to run the installer in order to copy the game in. Of course, just because you install a game as Administrator doesn't mean it runs as Administrator. Many older games weren't coded all that well, and will just outright crash when they're unable to write data. For many games, this happens in the opening sequence when it tries to write it's initial configuration files.

This means that most older games won't work in the default installation directory unless they are run with elevated permissions (Administrator) which is something you should never do. Games from the Windows XP and older era should be installed in a directory other than "Program Files" or "Program Files (x86)". I usually just make a directory called "games" off the root of the drive and install them there. Then they don't need any special permissions to do their business.
